passage:
For six months, Dilnaz had fallen asleep with her phone on her pillow and the chat with Arman still open. He wrote poems. He remembered her exam dates. He never managed a video call: his camera was broken, then the network in Dubai was bad, then his mother was ill.
On Thursday, in the Lucknow flat, her friend Seema quietly showed her a search result. Arman's photos belonged to a fitness trainer in Canada with a different name, a wife and two children.
Dilnaz didn't cry at first. She sat very still. Then she said, "How could I be so stupid?"
Seema sat beside her on the bed. "You're not stupid. You were kind, and someone used that on purpose. People who do this practise it."
Dilnaz pressed her face into Seema's shoulder. The grief was real, even if he wasn't.

qa.q: What excuses did Arman give for not video calling?
qa.a: His camera was broken, then the network in Dubai was bad, then his mother was ill.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling when she said "How could I be so stupid?"
qa.a: She felt shame and shock, blaming herself for trusting someone who wasn't real.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz do next, with Seema's help?
qa.a: She could stop contact, save the chats and report the profile, and keep talking to Seema or a counsellor about the grief instead of hiding it.

qa.q: How does Seema see what happened to Dilnaz?
qa.a: Seema sees Dilnaz as kind, not stupid, and puts the blame on the person who deceived her on purpose.

grounding: A young woman who spent six months loving Arman online, though he avoided every video call, feels grief and shame when the truth emerges, and a friend says she is not stupid.

passage:
"She cancelled again?" Asif asked, handing Raghav a glass of chai on the hostel terrace.
"Her train got delayed. Third time." Raghav stared at his phone. "Ishani says next month for sure."
"Five months, man. Not one video call?"
"She's shy on camera. I told you."
Asif hesitated, then turned his own phone around. "Someone in my class got the same messages. Same poems, same shy on camera, from a different name. The pictures are a model's."
Raghav read it. His jaw worked. "I told her about my dad's surgery. I told her things I haven't told you."
"I know."
"I'm such an idiot."
"You're not. You were honest with someone who wasn't. That's on them."
Raghav put the chai down. "It still feels like someone died."
"Then it's okay to feel that," Asif said, and sat down beside him.

qa.q: Where are Raghav and Asif talking?
qa.a: They are talking on the hostel terrace, over chai.

qa.q: What does Raghav mean when he says it feels like someone died?
qa.a: He feels real grief for the person he believed in, even though she never existed as he knew her.

qa.q: What could Raghav do now that he knows?
qa.a: He could stop replying, report the profile, send nothing more, and keep talking to Asif or a counsellor about the hurt and shame.

qa.q: What was it like for Asif to show Raghav the proof?
qa.a: Asif hesitated, likely dreading the hurt it would cause, but chose honesty and then stayed beside Raghav instead of mocking him.

grounding: A young man invested in Ishani, who always avoided calls and meetings, feels grief and shame when Asif reveals the truth, and is told it is not his fault.

passage:
January. Darshan met "Meher" on a music forum. She sent long, beautiful messages every night. She had a camera problem, so no video calls. Darshan didn't mind. He felt understood for the first time in years.
April. They talked about the future. When he suggested meeting in Delhi, her mother fell sick. Then her job changed. Then her phone broke. In May, she asked him for money for a hospital bill. His friend Sahil frowned. "Have you ever seen her face moving? Even once?"
June. Sahil helped him run her photos through an image search. They belonged to an actress from another country. The account vanished the same night Darshan asked about it.
Darshan sat on the floor of his room, grieving someone who never existed, and hating himself. "How was I so stupid?"
Sahil sat beside him. "You weren't stupid. You were kind. They lie for a living." Then he helped him report the account to the cyber cell.

qa.q: Who did Meher's photos actually belong to?
qa.a: They belonged to an actress from another country.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel when the truth came out?
qa.a: Darshan felt grief for someone who never existed, and deep shame, calling himself stupid.

qa.q: What did Sahil do that helped Darshan?
qa.a: Sahil suggested checking her photos, told Darshan he wasn't stupid but kind, and helped him report the account to the cyber cell.

qa.q: How does Sahil see the deception?
qa.a: Sahil sees it as the work of practised liars, not a failing of Darshan's intelligence.

grounding: It shows a young adult who invested months of feeling in an online partner who avoided video calls, feeling grief and shame when the truth emerged.

passage:
Samir, you think you're the only one who's ever been fooled? Sit. Let your Ira Phuppo tell you about my pen friend.
I was twenty. There was no internet then, only letters. A pen friend from Shillong wrote to me for two years. Such letters. Poems, pressed flowers, plans for our life. He never sent a photograph. His camera was broken, then lost, then stolen.
I told my friends I was in love. I turned down a proposal from a very nice boy because of those letters.
Then my cousin, visiting Shillong, went to the address. It was a printing press. The owner's son, fifty years old and married, had been writing to many girls.
I cried for a month. Not only for him. For myself, for being so foolish.
But Samir, I wasn't foolish. I was hopeful. Being fooled by a liar says something about him, not about you.

qa.q: What did young Ira's cousin find at the address in Shillong?
qa.a: It was a printing press.

qa.q: How did young Ira feel after the truth came out?
qa.a: Ira felt grief and shame, crying for a month and feeling foolish for believing him.

qa.q: What turning point in the story revealed the truth?
qa.a: Ira's cousin visited the address in Shillong and discovered it was a printing press run by a married man.

qa.q: How might the nice boy Ira turned down have felt?
qa.a: He may have felt disappointed and confused, not knowing that Ira was holding on to letters from someone false.

grounding: An aunt recalls falling for a pen friend she never met who avoided photographs, and the grief and shame when the truth emerged.

passage:
The overnight bus from Bhopal reached Pune at seven in the morning, and it was raining hard. Zainab stood under the bus stand roof with her bag, waiting for Yash.
They had talked for eight months. He always had a reason not to video call: bad network, shy, then a hostel rule. But he'd promised he'd be at the stand with an umbrella.
By eight, he hadn't come. His number was switched off. By nine, his profile had disappeared.
Zainab stood shivering, surrounded by strangers, her face hot with shame. She'd told her college friends she was meeting her boyfriend. She'd lied to her parents about a "college trip."
She called her friend Farah, crying. Farah said, "Listen. You are not stupid. Someone lied to you on purpose. Go to the ticket counter and take the next bus home. I'll stay on the phone."
Zainab bought a ticket. On the long ride back, she let herself grieve.

qa.q: What time did the bus reach Pune?
qa.a: At seven in the morning.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel waiting at the bus stand?
qa.a: Zainab felt shame and grief, her face hot and body shivering, realising she had been deceived after eight months.

qa.q: What did Farah advise, and why did it help?
qa.a: Farah reassured Zainab she wasn't stupid and told her to take the next bus home, staying on the phone, which got her safely back.

qa.q: How does Farah see what happened to Zainab?
qa.a: Farah sees it as someone lying to Zainab on purpose, not a sign of Zainab's stupidity.

grounding: It shows a young adult who invested in an online partner who avoided video calls, left waiting in the rain, feeling grief and shame.

passage: In their Bandra flat, Maria found Madhuri on the balcony floor at midnight, phone face down. For five months Madhuri had talked every night with Neil, an engineer in Dubai. He sent poems, remembered her mother's birthday, and always had a reason not to video call: bad network, a broken camera, a night shift. Tonight Maria's image search, done on a hunch, had shown his photos belonged to a fitness trainer in Brazil. "I planned our wedding in my head," Madhuri whispered. "How can someone so smart be so stupid?" Maria sat down beside her. "You're not stupid. You were kind and honest with someone who wasn't. People who do this practise on thousands." Madhuri cried, for a man who had never existed and for the five months. In the morning Maria stayed with her while she reported the profile and called her elder sister.

qa.q: What reasons did Neil give for not video calling?
qa.a: Bad network, a broken camera and a night shift.

qa.q: What does Madhuri's question about being so stupid reveal?
qa.a: Madhuri feels ashamed as well as grief-stricken, blaming herself while mourning the man and the five months.

qa.q: What is helpful about Maria's response?
qa.a: Maria sits with Madhuri, says being deceived is not stupidity, and stays while Madhuri reports the profile and calls her sister.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt when the search showed the photos belonged to someone else?
qa.a: Maria likely felt worried and sad for Madhuri, knowing the news would hurt, which is why Maria stayed close.

grounding: Shows a young adult who invested feelings in an online partner who avoided video calls, and feels grief and shame when the truth comes out.
